questions.title: Total body water is lower in adult females than males
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Body Fluids > Total Body Water
questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly compares total body water, as a percentage of body weight, between average adult males and females?

options.A: It is exactly equal in both sexes
options.B: It is generally greater in adult females
options.C: It is generally lower in adult females
options.D: It depends entirely on daily fluid intake, not sex

explanations.A: Incorrect. Total body water differs consistently between the sexes on average; it is not equal, because body composition (fat versus lean tissue) differs between average adult males and females.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the true relationship — total body water as a fraction of weight is lower, not greater, in adult females, because adipose tissue contains little water.
explanations.C: Correct. Adult females carry a proportionally higher percentage of body fat, and adipose tissue holds very little water compared with lean tissue, so total body water as a fraction of body weight (about 50%) is lower than in adult males (about 60%). The same logic explains why total body water, as a fraction of weight, falls with rising adiposity in either sex, not only when comparing the sexes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While hydration status can shift body water short-term, the average sex difference reflects underlying body composition (fat versus lean mass), not day-to-day fluid intake.

questions.learning_objective: State that total body water as a percentage of body weight is lower in adult females than adult males, and attribute the difference to higher average body fat, not to fluid intake or renal handling.
